strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and practical problem: understanding the local routing consistency of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to optimize expert offloading on memory-constrained devices.
The proposed metrics, Segment Routing Best Performance (SRP) and Segment Cache Best Hit Rate (SCH), are mathematically rigorous, well-defined, and accompanied by formal proofs in the appendix.

The empirical evaluation is exceptionally comprehensive, analyzing 20 diverse, publicly available MoE models spanning different scales (3B to 57B parameters) and architectural designs (e.g., shared experts, layer-skipping MoE, different routing strategies).

The paper offers actionable design and deployment insights, such as pointing out that MoE-on-every-layer configurations without shared experts lead to superior local routing consistency, and identifying 2x the size of active parameters as an optimal cache size.
weaknesses: The paper lacks real-world, end-to-end hardware latency measurements. Although it shows high correlation with standard caching algorithms, showing the actual speedups (e.g., in tokens per second) on an offloading system (such as Fiddler or MoE-Infinity) would make the system-level claims even more convincing.
There is an incomplete sentence at the end of the abstract: 'We publish the code for replicating experiments a', which suggests a minor oversight in final proofreading.

strengths: Extensive and Diverse Model Analysis: The paper evaluates an impressive range of 20 diverse MoE models (ranging from 3B to 57B parameters) covering multiple families (SwitchTransformers, Mixtral, Qwen, DeepSeek, OLMoE, etc.), ensuring the findings are robust and highly generalizable.

Well-Formulated Metrics: The definitions of Segment Routing Best Performance (SRP) and Segment Cache Best Hit Rate (SCH) are mathematically sound, and the paper provides rigorous proofs (e.g., for Equation 3 and Equation 4 in the Appendix).

Valuable Architectural Insights: The analysis reveals interesting and actionable insights, such as the negative impact of shared experts/dense layers on routing consistency, and the finding that domain specialization contributes significantly more to routing consistency than vocabulary specialization.

Comprehensive Appendix: The authors provide extensive additional evaluations in the appendix (such as base vs. post-trained comparison, position-wise analysis, perplexity correlations), which strengthens the paper's claims.
weaknesses: Lack of Real-world System Performance Evaluation: Although the paper focuses heavily on the implications for expert offloading, it lacks actual system measurements (e.g., end-to-end inference latency, memory usage, or throughput on a memory-constrained device) to validate the proposed findings. Relying purely on theoretical/simulated cache hit rates (SCH) leaves a gap between the metrics and actual wall-clock speedups.

Missing Co-Design Validation: The paper provides architectural suggestions (e.g., applying MoE on every layer, avoiding shared experts) to improve routing consistency. However, it does not validate these claims by training/fine-tuning a model to demonstrate that optimizing for these characteristics maintains downstream accuracy while improving offloading efficiency in practice.

Incomplete Abstract & Text Typos: The abstract ends abruptly with a cut-off sentence: '...publish the code for replicating experiments a'. There are also minor formatting issues like extremely small fonts in Figures 3, 4, 10, 11, and 12, which makes reading the labels very difficult.

Incremental Algorithmic Novelty: The paper is primarily analytical. The metrics (SRP, SCH) are minor variations of standard sequence classification metrics (F1) and oracle caching hit rates. While the empirical study is valuable, the algorithmic or methodological novelty is relatively limited.

strengths: Proposes two well-defined, mathematically grounded, and complementary metrics (SRP and SCH) to quantitatively measure local routing consistency in MoEs.
Conducts a massive, systematic empirical evaluation involving 20 diverse MoE models ranging from 3B to 57B parameters, providing a comprehensive landscape of existing MoEs.

Provides valuable, actionable architectural and system-level insights (e.g., MoE on every layer without shared experts increases consistency; a cache size of ~2x the active parameters is the optimal sweet spot).
Presents rigorous mathematical proofs for the optimal thresholds of the metrics in the appendix, ensuring the soundness of the definitions.
The paper is very well-written, clearly structured, and includes extensive analysis on expert specialization (domain vs. vocabulary).
weaknesses: The evaluation uses a sequence length of 512 tokens, which is relatively short compared to modern long-context scenarios (e.g., 8k to 128k+). It remains unclear how local routing consistency scales or shifts under very long context lengths or major topic changes.
The paper is primarily analytical and does not implement a real-world optimized offloading system/scheduler or report actual wall-clock speedups (e.g., latency, throughput) on physical hardware.
There is a minor typo/incomplete sentence at the end of the abstract ('We publish the code for replicating experiments a').

strengths: Highly relevant and timely topic focused on understanding and optimizing the local routing consistency of MoE models for memory-efficient expert offloading on edge devices.
Comprehensive empirical analysis covering 20 diverse, real-world MoE LLMs (ranging from 3B to 57B parameters), providing a solid foundation for the observations.
Meticulous validation using custom-trained toy models to isolate and confirm specific architectural/training factors (such as load balancing loss, shared experts, and expert granularity).
Well-motivated and mathematically sound metrics: Segment Routing Best Performance (SRP) and Segment Cache Best Hit Rate (SCH), with formal definitions and proofs provided in the appendix.
Valuable design guidelines for future MoE architectures to ensure they are offloading-friendly without sacrificing global load balance.
weaknesses: The main body of the paper lacks end-to-end throughput and latency evaluation (e.g., tokens/second) on actual hardware. While theoretical discussions and a brief analysis are present in Appendix F, concrete benchmarks with existing offloading frameworks would significantly strengthen the work.

The proposed SCH metric assumes an oracle cache with look-ahead capabilities. Although the authors show high correlation with LRU/LFU, a deeper analysis of how practical online prediction algorithms perform under different routing consistencies would bridge the gap further.

The trade-off between model performance (perplexity/downstream accuracy) and local routing consistency is not fully fleshed out. For instance, while 'NoLB' has high SRP, its training convergence or final performance trade-offs could be discussed in greater depth.

strengths: Extensive and Systematic Evaluation: The paper evaluates 20 real-world MoE models spanning different families (including Mixtral, DeepSeek, Qwen, LLaMA-MoE, and SwitchTransformers) and sizes (3B to 57B). This is an exceptionally broad study compared to prior works that only look at one or two models.

Causal Analysis via Pre-trained Toy Models: To isolate the architectural and training factors that influence local routing consistency, the authors pre-train a series of 1.43B parameter MoE models from scratch with controlled variations (e.g., load balancing weight, shared experts, active expert count). This provides robust empirical backing.

Well-Formulated Metrics: The introduction of Segment Routing Best Performance (SRP) and Segment Cache Best Hit Rate (SCH) provides complementary analytical tools. SRP offers a parameter-free theoretical upper bound of local consistency, while SCH bridges the gap to realistic on-device caching constraints.

Actionable Design Guidelines: The paper provides clear recommendations for future MoE designs intended for edge deployment, such as avoiding shared experts if offloading is anticipated, leveraging domain specialization to maintain both local consistency and global load balance, and sizing the cache at approximately 2x the active expert capacity.
weaknesses: Lack of End-to-End System Latency/Throughput Benchmarks: Although the paper shows that the proposed SCH metric highly correlates with LRU/LFU cache hit rates, it does not demonstrate actual hardware metrics (such as token-per-second throughput or token latency) on real memory-constrained devices using an end-to-end offloading system (e.g., Fiddler or EdgeMoE).

Limited Analysis of Post-Training Methods: The claim that post-training (SFT, DPO) does not impact local routing consistency is evaluated on only three models. Since reinforcement learning (e.g., RLHF, GRPO) can dramatically change routing preferences, a broader investigation into RL-tuned models would strengthen this conclusion.

Informal Visualization in Figure 1: While Figure 1 is intuitive, the grid representation of expert activations is somewhat hard to read and could be presented in a more professional heatmap or line plot format.

strengths: Timely and highly practical topic: This work targets a critical bottleneck in deploying large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs on memory-constrained devices by systematically investigating 'local routing consistency' for expert offloading.

Extensive empirical analysis: Evaluates 20 diverse, real-world MoE LLMs (ranging from SwitchTransformers to Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V2) and pretrains multiple controlled toy models to isolate and study specific architectural and training hyper-parameters (e.g., shared experts, load balance loss).

Rigorously defined metrics: The proposed metrics (SRP and SCH) provide parameter-free and cache-aligned ways to quantify routing consistency, supported by formal definitions and mathematical proofs in the appendix.

Valuable design insights: The paper delivers several practical takeaways for MoE system-model co-design, such as the negative impact of shared experts on routing consistency, the trade-off with local load balancing, the positive contribution of domain-specialized experts, and a concrete recommendation for cache sizing (2x active experts).
weaknesses: Limited real-world hardware throughput evaluation: The connection to actual system performance (such as decoding latency or throughput on edge/consumer hardware) is primarily discussed qualitatively or in simulated terms in Appendix F. More concrete latency and throughput benchmarks on real devices would significantly strengthen the practical system claims.

Reliance on simplified/oracle caching models: While SCH is correlated with standard LRU/LFU cache policies, state-of-the-art expert offloading systems (e.g., Fiddler, EdgeMoE) often employ more sophisticated prefetching and predictive heuristics. It is not fully verified how closely SRP/SCH translate to the actual efficiency improvements in these advanced deployment frameworks.
